solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Orderly snubbed close to end of shift

indicators.note: to snub is literally to cut short, so the word loses its tail
the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is taken

explanation.surface: A hospital orderly is cold-shouldered as their shift winds down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orderly' reads as a hospital porter, but it is the adjective: tidy, in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tidy, well-kept room is both orderly and neat.

clue.text: No aid for golfer carrying bag around — that takes money

indicators.note: NO TEE holds the bag inside it

parts.note: NO + TEE, the peg a golfer sets the ball on

indicators.note: to turn around is to face the other way, so the bag's letters run backwards

parts.note: a sac is a bag, reversed to CAS

explanation.surface: A golfer without a tee lugs a bag about, and apparently that costs money.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'that takes money' sound like a comment on golf; it is the definition, a wallet that takes banknotes.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a notecase, an old word for a wallet, is made to hold banknotes.

clue.text: Unpleasant atmosphere? My aircon's bust

indicators.note: broken, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The office air conditioning has died and the air is stuffy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Atmosphere' pushes toward heat and stale air; the atmosphere meant is bad feeling between people.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrimony is bitterness that makes the mood in a room unpleasant.

clue.text: Suits Palace and takes over the side

parts.note: a royal court, the palace and its household
a boat that ships water takes it in over the side

explanation.surface: A football club called Palace picks up a whole team in a takeover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suits' looks like a verb or clothing; it is the plural noun for wooings, as a suitor pays suit.
explanation.definitionFit: A suit is a courtship, a man's formal wooing of a woman.

clue.text: Former head of Unilever plugs Lynx no longer

indicators.note: the head of a word is its top, the first letter

parts.note: once = former, as in the once king

explanation.surface: A former Unilever boss promotes Lynx, the body spray the company makes.
explanation.walkthrough: Lynx is a Unilever deodorant, so the surface is a business story. 'No longer' says the sense is obsolete: ounce once meant a lynx, and now names the snow leopard.
explanation.definitionFit: Ounce was an old name for the lynx before it passed to the snow leopard.

clue.text: Caribbean music artist controlling urge to record standing on head

indicators.note: the artist holds the urge inside
in a down entry, upside down reads bottom to top

parts.note: to egg on is to urge
to note is to record, turned over to ETON

explanation.surface: A musician resists the itch to make a record while doing a headstand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music artist' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'music'.
explanation.definitionFit: Reggaeton is a dance music from Puerto Rico and the Caribbean.

clue.text: Mike Brown, rogue Conservative MP, again admits plan to discredit opposition?

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so Brown lets Mike inside it
wayward, so those letters are rearranged

parts.note: to sear is to brown meat
Mike is M in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A rogue Tory MP called Mike Brown is caught confessing to another dirty-tricks plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mike Brown' reads as a name; split it. Brown admits Mike to give SMEAR, and the rest rearranges to CAMPAIGN.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a smear is a damaging slur, and a campaign an organised drive, so the whole is a plan to blacken opponents.

clue.text: Bar unending permits for small arms

indicators.note: with its last letter removed

explanation.surface: An endless pub licence covers handguns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small arms' is weaponry on the surface; here the arms are of the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: An inlet is a small arm of the sea reaching into the land.

clue.text: Older central sections of museum painted maize yellow

indicators.note: take the middle of each of the next three words

parts.note: or is gold or yellow in heraldry

explanation.surface: Parts of an old museum were given a coat of corn-yellow paint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yellow' is not a fourth word to take the centre of; it gives OR whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the elder of two people is the senior one.

clue.text: Gives up and retires

definitions.meaning: hands over to the police, as a fugitive surrenders
retires for the night, goes to bed

explanation.surface: Someone quits and steps down from work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retires' suggests leaving a job; the sense needed is going to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn in is both to hand over or surrender and to go to bed.

clue.text: Fine journalist entering area around NY museum shows alarm

parts.note: the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York

explanation.surface: A good reporter walks into a district near a New York gallery and sounds panicky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shows alarm' reads as a verb phrase; 'shows' only links, and 'alarm' is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the ceiling device that shrieks at smoke is one kind of alarm.

clue.text: Sort of girl men bug

indicators.note: to sort letters is to rearrange them

explanation.surface: A certain kind of woman irritates men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' reads as a verb, to annoy; it is the noun, a fault in a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A gremlin is an unexplained fault or bug in a system.

clue.text: America led by unnoble sort these days

parts.note: a commoner has no noble title

explanation.surface: The United States is now run by a man of no breeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Led by' puts COMMONER before A. 'These days' is fair because the Common Era is the dating system we live in now.
explanation.definitionFit: The Common Era is the present era of dating, CE, our days.

clue.text: Bring port round at 19:30?

indicators.note: to go round something is to encircle it

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro, the Brazilian port

explanation.surface: Pass the port around at half past seven in the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 19:30 looks like a clock time for after-dinner port; read the colon as a ratio, nineteen to thirty. The question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: 19:30 is written like a ratio, one number set against another.

clue.text: Basque place without French beans? I mostly ate nuts

indicators.note: most but not all of the word, so its last letter is dropped
crazy, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone in a Basque town, denied their French beans, ate nearly everything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French beans' reads as a vegetable; 'French' belongs with 'without' and the beans go into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: San Sebastian is a city in the Basque Country of northern Spain.

clue.text: Husband is enthralled by spinning trapdoor spider?

indicators.note: held captive inside the other letters
turning, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man is captivated by a trapdoor spider spinning its web.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trapdoor spider' is a real creature, which hides the split; the question mark says a spider is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiders are arthropods, jointed-legged invertebrates.

clue.text: Spooner's father wagers sums he won't see again

indicators.note: swap the opening sounds, as Rev. Spooner did

parts.note: a father is a dad; it takes the B from the next word
wagers are bets; it takes the D from the word before

explanation.surface: A father's gambling has lost money he'll never get back.
explanation.walkthrough: DAD BETS with its first sounds swapped becomes BAD DEBTS; the B of debts is silent, so the sounds match.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad debts are sums owed that will never be repaid.

clue.text: Fully confident ecstasy's consumed in much reduced quantity

indicators.note: swallowed inside the other piece

parts.note: far less = a much smaller amount

explanation.surface: Someone high on E feels sure of themselves after taking a smaller dose.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': ecstasy is consumed in FAR LESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearless means entirely without fear, fully confident.

clue.text: Succeed fitting stiff in grave?

indicators.note: to fit one thing into another is to insert it
the piece goes inside, completing 'fitting ... in'

parts.note: to succeed someone is to replace them
to stiff someone is to cheat them, a sting

explanation.surface: Getting a corpse to fit in a grave counts as a success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' looks like a corpse, which the grave suits; it is the verb, to cheat. The question mark marks the grave as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A grave is a resting place, where the dead lie.

clue.text: Pretentious type upside-down next to sloth in small tree

indicators.note: in a down entry, reads bottom to top

parts.note: the ai is a three-toed sloth

explanation.surface: A snob hangs upside down beside a sloth in a little tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The ai is the crossword's usual sloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonsai is a tree kept tiny by pruning.

clue.text: One inclined to accept eco-friendly car to overhaul

indicators.note: the ramp takes the car in

explanation.surface: Someone willing to take an electric car in for repairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One inclined' reads as a willing person; it is a sloping thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: giving a tired business a thorough makeover is both revamping and overhauling it.

clue.text: Seb Coe, ignoring cold, running with thick protective layer?

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out of account
in motion, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder once C is removed

explanation.surface: Seb Coe, the British Olympic runner, goes out in the cold with thermal gear.
explanation.walkthrough: The thick protective layer is fat, not clothing; the question mark admits the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means very fat, with a thick layer of body fat.

clue.text: Balance cue, keeping focus on black

indicators.note: the cue holds the letter inside

parts.note: a cue is a prompt, a reminder

indicators.note: the focus of something is its centre, so take the middle letter

explanation.surface: A snooker player steadies the cue while lining up the black ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The snooker picture hides the money sense of 'balance', what is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from accounting: the balance still owed is what remains after payments.

clue.text: Inspection of car seat regularly part of service

parts.note: the MOT is Britain's yearly roadworthiness test for cars

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: Checking the car seat is part of the vehicle's service.
explanation.walkthrough: The service is a church one, not a garage one: a motet is sung in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a choral piece sung as part of a church service.

clue.text: Consultants finally improve the look of new business

indicators.note: at the end, so only the last letter of the word is used

parts.note: to tart up is British slang for smartening something up

explanation.surface: Consultants at last smarten up the image of a young company.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a sentence about branding consultants.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the word describes a young company just starting to trade.

clue.text: Sound made by nail penetrating box

indicators.note: to penetrate is to pierce and go inside

parts.note: the box is British slang for television, the tele
to nail a thief is to nab him

explanation.surface: The noise when a nail is driven through a crate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' reads as a noise; it is the adjective, as in a sound argument.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenable position is sound, able to be defended.

clue.text: Tax worker avoids crucial task

indicators.note: to avoid something is to keep clear of it, so the worker is left out

explanation.surface: An employee dodges a vital job at tax time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax worker' looks like a taxman; the definition is 'Tax' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: An import duty is a tax charged on goods brought into a country.

clue.text: Watering hole opening late in current circumstances

indicators.note: late means dead, so the opening letter is gone

explanation.surface: A bar opens after hours in the present situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening late' reads as a pub keeping late hours; late means departed, so the opening letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: As is means in the present state, without changes.
